difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one obvious gap. The argument infers illness from symptom without considering alternative causes.
stimulus: Physician: All patients who came to my clinic with persistent cough were treated with antibiotics. Every one of them recovered within two weeks. Therefore, the antibiotics must have caused the recovery.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the physician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics are the only available treatment for persistent cough.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients' recovery would not have occurred without the antibiotic treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent cough is a serious condition that requires medical intervention.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two weeks is the typical time frame for recovery from any illness treated with antibiotics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patients followed the physician's treatment instructions exactly.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that without antibiotics, recovery would not have happened. If negated—the patients could have recovered without treatment—the conclusion that antibiotics caused the recovery falls apart.
explanations.A: Too strong; the argument needs only that this treatment worked, not that it's the only option.
explanations.C: Irrelevant to whether antibiotics caused the recovery.
explanations.D: Timeline support is not required; the argument just needs the causal link.
explanations.E: Patient compliance is not part of the causal claim being made.

difficultyReason: Simple one-premise argument with gap between observation and conclusion about categorization.
stimulus: Economist: The stock market rose sharply after the new tax policy was announced. Therefore, investors believe the new policy is good for the economy.
questionStem: The economist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rising stock market is always a reliable indicator of economic health.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rise in the stock market was caused by investor belief in the policy's positive effects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new tax policy will actually improve the economy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Investors always behave rationally when trading stocks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No other factors besides the tax policy announcement caused the stock market to rise.

explanations.correct: The argument links the market rise to investor belief about the policy. Negate B: if the rise was not caused by belief in the policy, the inference collapses. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Too broad; the argument is about what investors believe, not general reliability.
explanations.C: The argument is about investor belief, not actual economic outcomes.
explanations.D: Rationality is not required; investors could believe for any reason.
explanations.E: Out of scope—the argument is about the link between policy and belief, not about competing causes.

difficultyReason: Direct single-premise argument with transparent gap between observation and categorical claim.
stimulus: Literary critic: Every novel by Martinez that I have read is beautifully written. Therefore, all of Martinez's novels are beautifully written.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Martinez has written more novels than the critic has read.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The critic's personal taste in literature is shared by most readers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novels the critic has read are representative of Martinez's entire body of work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beauty in writing is an objective quality that can be measured.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The critic is more knowledgeable about literature than other critics.

explanations.correct: To infer all novels from some novels, the read sample must be representative. Negate C: the read novels are not representative—then the conclusion doesn't follow. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Confirms the gap but is not itself the assumption bridging it.
explanations.B: Reader agreement is irrelevant to whether all of Martinez's novels are beautiful.
explanations.D: Objectivity of beauty is not required for the inference.
explanations.E: The critic's standing relative to others is out of scope.

difficultyReason: Single-premise argument drawing a causal conclusion from mere correlation.
stimulus: Nutritionist: People who eat more leafy green vegetables have lower rates of heart disease. Therefore, eating leafy greens prevents heart disease.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in developed nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who eat leafy greens do not differ from others in ways that independently reduce heart disease risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leafy green vegetables contain more nutrients than any other type of vegetable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A diet of only leafy greens would prevent heart disease entirely.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The correlation between leafy greens and lower heart disease has been observed in all populations.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from correlation to causation. B assumes no confounding variables (e.g., leafy-green eaters exercise more). Negate B: they do differ in independent ways—then the greens may not be the cause. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Prevalence of heart disease is not relevant to the causal claim.
explanations.C: Nutrient density relative to other vegetables is irrelevant.
explanations.D: Too strong; the argument needs only that greens help, not that they're sufficient.
explanations.E: Universal correlation is not required; the argument concerns a general causal relationship.

difficultyReason: Simple argument with transparent gap between two premises and conclusion about attribution.
stimulus: Detective: The theft occurred while the store was closed. The only employee with a key is Rosa. Therefore, Rosa committed the theft.
questionStem: The detective's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rosa was in the store when the theft occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theft is a more serious crime than other offenses Rosa might have committed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No one other than Rosa could have had access to the store.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rosa had a motive to steal from the store.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store's security system was not functioning at the time of the theft.

explanations.correct: For access to imply culpability, no one else could have accessed the store. Negate C: others could have accessed it—then access doesn't point to Rosa. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Presence during the theft is confirmed by C without being explicitly stated.
explanations.B: Crime severity is irrelevant to identifying the perpetrator.
explanations.D: Motive is not part of the access-based reasoning.
explanations.E: Security status is out of scope; the argument is about key access.

difficultyReason: Straightforward inference from one premise to conclusion, with a single implicit assumption.
stimulus: Engineer: The bridge's steel cables have not been inspected in ten years. Therefore, the bridge is unsafe and must be closed.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Steel cables that have not been inspected for ten years are likely to have developed defects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bridge was safe when the cables were last inspected ten years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular inspection of steel cables can prevent all bridge failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No bridge with uninspected cables has ever remained safe for long.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bridge closures are the only effective way to prevent accidents.

explanations.correct: The argument links lack of inspection to unsafety. This requires assuming that uninspected cables are likely defective. Negate A: old cables could be fine—then the inference to unsafety fails. A is necessary.
explanations.B: Historical safety status is not what the argument depends on.
explanations.C: Prevention of all failures is too strong; the argument needs only that inspection matters.
explanations.D: Absolutist claim not required; the argument needs only that uninspected cables pose risk.
explanations.E: Whether closure is the only remedy is irrelevant to whether the bridge is unsafe.

difficultyReason: Basic argument with one premise and a conclusion that requires bridging a simple conceptual gap.
stimulus: Linguist: Children who grow up hearing two languages learn to read earlier than children exposed to only one language. Thus, bilingualism helps children develop reading skills.
questionStem: The linguist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: Learning two languages is more difficult than learning one language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early reading ability is causally linked to later academic success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The early reading advantage of bilingual children is due to their bilingual exposure, not other factors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilingual parents are more attentive to their children's education than monolingual parents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reading is more important than other language skills in child development.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a correlation between bilingualism and early reading. C rules out confounds (educated parents, socioeconomic factors). Negate C: the advantage comes from other factors—then bilingualism doesn't help. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Difficulty level is irrelevant to whether bilingualism helps.
explanations.B: Later outcomes are not part of the argument's reasoning.
explanations.D: Parental attentiveness is a potential confound, but the argument doesn't explicitly address it.
explanations.E: Relative importance of reading vs. other skills is out of scope.

difficultyReason: Single-premise inference with an obvious and testable gap via negation.
stimulus: Historian: Ancient Rome's collapse was caused by barbarian invasions. Rome had no standing armies large enough to repel them. Therefore, Rome was doomed once the invasions began.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barbarian invasions were unexpected by Roman leadership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rome could not have successfully defended itself against the invasions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Barbarian invasions were the primary cause of Rome's decline in other ancient civilizations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Military technology favored the barbarians over the Romans.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rome had previously repelled invasions using the same military forces.

explanations.correct: The argument claims inadequate armies meant doom. This assumes the armies could not have succeeded. Negate B: Rome could have defended—then insufficient army size doesn't doom the state. B is necessary.
explanations.C: Other civilizations' experiences are out of scope.
explanations.D: Technology advantage is one possible reason but not a necessary assumption.
explanations.E: Past success is not required; previous repulsion doesn't determine future capability.

difficultyReason: Straightforward argument with one evident gap between evidence and categorical conclusion.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Wetlands in the region have been drained to build housing developments. Species that depend on wetlands are now disappearing. Therefore, the loss of wetlands is causing the species decline.
questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Housing developments are built with no concern for environmental impact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The species' disappearance is not caused by hunting, pollution, or other factors unrelated to wetland loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wetlands are more important to species survival than any other type of habitat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All species in the region depend on wetlands for their survival.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Housing developments cause more habitat loss than any other human activity.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from temporal and ecological correlation. B assumes no confounding causes. Negate B: other factors cause the decline—then wetland loss isn't the cause. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Developer intent is irrelevant to the causal claim.
explanations.C: Relative importance is not required; wetlands need only be relevant.
explanations.D: All species need not depend on wetlands; the argument concerns species that do.
explanations.E: Comparative impact of development vs. other activities is out of scope.

difficultyReason: Simple inference from policy implementation to expected outcome, with a clear causal assumption.
stimulus: Policy advisor: The city implemented a curfew for teenagers. Youth crime has since decreased by 20 percent. Therefore, the curfew reduced youth crime.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 20 percent decrease in youth crime is significant enough to warrant the curfew policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Youth crime would not have decreased by 20 percent without the curfew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Curfews are more effective at reducing crime than other police interventions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decrease in youth crime affected all demographic groups equally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Police enforcement of the curfew was consistent throughout the city.

explanations.correct: To attribute the crime decrease to the curfew, the argument must assume the decrease wouldn't have happened otherwise. Negate B: crime would have fallen anyway—then the curfew didn't cause the decrease. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Significance is a separate evaluative question, not a causal assumption.
explanations.C: Relative effectiveness vs. alternatives is out of scope.
explanations.D: Equal demographic impact is not required for the causal inference.
explanations.E: Consistency of enforcement affects strength but not the causal logic itself.
